difficultyReason: Textbook ad hominem in pure form. The columnist dismisses a study by attacking the researcher's character rather than engaging with the evidence. The correct answer is the only one that describes that move; trap choices point at peripheral weaknesses.
stimulus: Health columnist: Dr. Reyes has just published a study claiming that daily consumption of green tea modestly reduces the risk of heart disease. But Dr. Reyes was fined two years ago for filing inaccurate expense reports at her previous university. Clearly, then, we have no reason to accept her conclusions about green tea.
questionStem: The reasoning in the health columnist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: rejects a claim by attacking the character of the person who made it rather than addressing the evidence for the claim

choices.label: B
choices.text: generalizes from a single study to a conclusion about all research on green tea

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats a condition sufficient for distrusting a researcher as also necessary for doing so

choices.label: D
choices.text: confuses a claim about heart disease risk with a claim about overall health outcomes

choices.label: E
choices.text: relies on a source whose expertise in the relevant field has not been established

explanations.correct: The columnist's only reason for rejecting the study is the researcher's past expense-report issue — a matter of personal conduct unrelated to her research on green tea. That is a textbook attack on the person rather than the argument.
explanations.B: The columnist never generalizes across studies; she rejects the one study she discusses.
explanations.C: No necessary/sufficient move is made; the columnist simply asserts grounds for distrust.
explanations.D: The argument stays on heart disease; no scope shift to overall health occurs.
explanations.E: The columnist doesn't question Dr. Reyes's expertise; she questions her character.

difficultyReason: Pure self-contradiction: the speaker affirms a universal claim and then exempts themselves from it in the same breath. The correct answer names the contradiction; trap answers describe plausible but unrelated flaws.
stimulus: Ethicist: It is always wrong to judge another person's actions without first hearing their reasons for acting as they did. That is why I can say with complete confidence that the council member who voted against the new park ordinance last night — I haven't spoken with her, but I've heard enough — acted wrongly and deserves public censure.
questionStem: The reasoning in the ethicist's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about a specific action from a general principle that was never defended

choices.label: B
choices.text: violates the very principle it asserts by judging an action without hearing the actor's reasons

choices.label: C
choices.text: confuses what is morally permissible with what is legally required

choices.label: D
choices.text: appeals to the opinions of unspecified others as if they were authoritative

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats a single instance of bad judgment as evidence of a broader pattern

explanations.correct: The ethicist states a universal rule — never judge without hearing reasons — and then, without hearing the council member's reasons, judges her action as wrong. The argument's conclusion is incompatible with its own stated premise.
explanations.A: The flaw isn't that the principle is undefended; it's that the ethicist's own conduct violates it.
explanations.C: No legal/moral distinction is drawn or conflated.
explanations.D: The hearsay ('I've heard enough') is a weakness but not the central structural flaw.
explanations.E: Only one action is judged; no pattern is alleged.

difficultyReason: Textbook correlation-to-causation move. Cities that raised transit spending saw ridership rise, and the analyst concludes the spending caused the rise. Correct answer names the move; traps target peripheral weaknesses.
stimulus: Transportation analyst: Cities that increased their public-transit spending by at least ten percent last year saw an average rise in ridership of seven percent. Cities that did not increase spending saw no such rise. The conclusion is clear: the additional spending is what drove ridership higher in the cities that raised their budgets.
questionStem: The reasoning in the transportation analyst's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: infers a causal relationship from evidence that establishes only a correlation

choices.label: B
choices.text: relies on a sample of cities that is too small to support a general conclusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: assumes without warrant that ridership is the most important measure of transit success

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizes from the behavior of a few cities to the behavior of all cities

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats a necessary condition for rising ridership as if it were sufficient

explanations.correct: The data show only that spending increases and ridership increases occurred together. The analyst leaps from that co-occurrence to the causal claim that the spending drove the ridership, without ruling out alternative explanations such as fuel prices, new employers, or population growth.
explanations.B: Sample size isn't raised as a problem in the stimulus and isn't the structural error.
explanations.C: The argument never ranks measures of success.
explanations.D: The conclusion is about the cities in question, not all cities.
explanations.E: No conditional move is made; the argument is causal, not conditional.

difficultyReason: Pure sufficient/necessary reversal. The statute makes a warrant sufficient for a lawful search; the attorney treats it as necessary. Correct answer names the reversal; traps offer plausible-sounding but wrong flaw labels.
stimulus: Defense attorney: Under our state's statute, if officers obtain a valid warrant before entering a residence, the search is lawful. The officers who entered my client's home last week did not obtain a warrant beforehand. Therefore, the search of my client's home was unlawful.
questionStem: The reasoning in the defense attorney's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a sufficient condition for a lawful search as if it were a necessary condition

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejects a claim on the basis of the character of the person making it

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about a specific case from a statistic about all cases

choices.label: D
choices.text: assumes without warrant that the officers acted in bad faith

choices.label: E
choices.text: relies on a legal principle that has never been tested in court

explanations.correct: The statute says that a warrant is one way to make a search lawful — a sufficient condition. Other exceptions (consent, exigent circumstances, plain view) may also render a search lawful. The attorney wrongly treats the warrant as the only path to lawfulness, converting a sufficient condition into a necessary one.
explanations.B: No one's character is attacked; the argument is about legal conditions.
explanations.E: The testing history of the principle is not at issue.

difficultyReason: Classic hasty generalization. Two sampled lakes, conclusion about all lakes in the region. Correct answer names the unrepresentative-sample move; traps describe other flaws the argument does not commit.
stimulus: Biologist: Researchers tested two lakes in the Fenwick watershed last summer and found elevated mercury levels in fish from both. It follows that fish from every lake throughout the entire Fenwick watershed are contaminated with elevated mercury and should not be eaten.
questionStem: The reasoning in the biologist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a sweeping conclusion about an entire region from a sample that may not be representative of it

choices.label: B
choices.text: mistakes a correlation between mercury and fish habitat for a causal relationship

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to distinguish between recreational and commercial fishing practices

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes without justification that mercury is the only contaminant worth testing for

choices.label: E
choices.text: uses the ambiguous term 'elevated' in two distinct senses

explanations.correct: Two lakes cannot, without further support, stand in for every lake in a watershed. The biologist leaps from a very small sample to a sweeping claim about all lakes in the region, an unrepresentative-sample flaw.
explanations.B: No causal claim is being defended; the claim is simply that the fish are contaminated.
explanations.C: The argument is about fish across the watershed, not about fishing practices.
explanations.D: The argument does not claim mercury is the only contaminant; it only claims mercury is elevated.
explanations.E: 'Elevated' is used consistently throughout the stimulus.

difficultyReason: Pure appeal to ignorance. Because no one has proved the device fails, the CEO concludes it works. Correct answer names the absence-of-evidence move; traps target unrelated flaw types.
stimulus: Tech CEO: Several independent researchers have tried, without success, to prove that our company's new encryption chip can be compromised by a remote attacker. Since no one has yet demonstrated a successful attack against the chip, we can conclude that our chip is secure against remote attacks.
questionStem: The reasoning in the tech CEO's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats the absence of evidence that a claim is false as if it established that the claim is true

choices.label: B
choices.text: generalizes from the experience of a few researchers to the capabilities of all possible attackers

choices.label: C
choices.text: confuses a necessary condition for a secure chip with a sufficient one

choices.label: D
choices.text: appeals to the authority of researchers whose credentials have not been verified

choices.label: E
choices.text: uses the term 'secure' in two different senses within the same argument

explanations.correct: No one has proved the chip can be cracked, so the CEO concludes it cannot be cracked. That inference treats the lack of a successful attack as positive evidence of security, which is a classic appeal-to-ignorance move.
explanations.B: This describes a sampling flaw the argument does not actually commit — the conclusion rests on absence of evidence, not on a sample.
explanations.D: The researchers' credentials are not invoked as support.
explanations.E: 'Secure' is used in a single sense throughout.

difficultyReason: Pure equivocation on the word 'argument.' Shifts between 'heated dispute' and 'reasoned case.' Correct answer names the two-senses move; traps offer flaw vocabulary that doesn't match.
stimulus: Linguistics student: Professor Yates said in lecture that a good argument never raises its voice. But last week in the department seminar, Professor Yates presented an argument that the dative case is disappearing from spoken Icelandic. So, by his own standard, Professor Yates's seminar presentation was not a good argument.
questionStem: The reasoning in the linguistics student's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: uses the word 'argument' in two different senses without acknowledging the shift

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejects a claim by attacking the credentials of the person who made it

choices.label: C
choices.text: generalizes from a single lecture to the professor's views across his entire career

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes without justification that raising one's voice is never appropriate

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats a property of a whole as if it were necessarily a property of each of its parts

explanations.correct: Professor Yates's maxim uses 'argument' to mean a heated dispute (the kind in which one might raise one's voice). The seminar sense of 'argument' is a reasoned case for a linguistic claim. The student silently trades one sense for the other to generate the contradiction.
explanations.B: No credentials are attacked; only a standard is invoked.
explanations.C: Only one lecture is referenced, not career-wide views.
explanations.D: The argument never addresses whether raising one's voice is appropriate.
explanations.E: No whole/part move appears in the stimulus.

difficultyReason: Appeal to inappropriate authority. A nutrition researcher is cited on a question of historical causation outside her expertise. Correct answer names the authority mismatch; traps describe other flaws.
stimulus: History student: Dr. Langford, who won a major national prize for her research on adolescent nutrition, recently stated in a podcast interview that the principal cause of the fall of the Western Roman Empire was a collapse in agricultural trade routes. Because Dr. Langford is a celebrated researcher, we should accept her account of Rome's decline.
questionStem: The reasoning in the history student's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: relies on the opinion of an authority whose expertise is in a field unrelated to the claim at issue

choices.label: B
choices.text: dismisses Dr. Langford's view by pointing to her work in an unrelated field

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats a sufficient condition for a historical cause as a necessary one

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a conclusion about an entire empire from information about a single region

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider that Dr. Langford's statements might have been taken out of context

explanations.correct: Dr. Langford is a specialist in adolescent nutrition, not in the history of Rome. The student supports a claim about Roman decline by citing her authority in an unrelated field, a classic appeal to inappropriate authority.
explanations.B: The argument accepts, not dismisses, Dr. Langford's view.
explanations.D: The claim is already about the empire, not a region.
explanations.E: Context isn't at issue; expertise is.

difficultyReason: Pure ignoring-alternatives flaw in false-dichotomy form. The council member insists it is cut services or raise property taxes. Correct answer names the unconsidered alternatives; traps describe unrelated flaws.
stimulus: City council member: To close next year's budget gap, we face a simple choice. Either we cut funding for the public library system, or we raise property taxes on every household in the city. Nobody on this council wants to cut library funding. Therefore, we have no option but to raise property taxes.
questionStem: The reasoning in the council member's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: presents only two options while giving no reason to think that no other options are available

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats a condition sufficient for closing the budget gap as if it were necessary

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about future budgets based solely on the current one

choices.label: D
choices.text: uses the term 'cut funding' in two different senses

choices.label: E
choices.text: rejects tax increases on the basis of the unpopularity of those who propose them

explanations.correct: The council member frames the decision as library cuts versus property-tax hikes, but a city has many other budget levers: sales taxes, user fees, spending cuts elsewhere, reserves, new revenue sources. The argument never justifies treating those two options as exhaustive.
explanations.B: No conditional move is made; the argument is a disjunction, not a conditional.
explanations.C: Only the next budget is at issue; no cross-year projection is made.
explanations.D: 'Cut funding' is used in one sense throughout.

difficultyReason: Pure whole-to-part conflation. Orchestra is excellent, therefore each member is excellent. Correct answer names the division-style flaw in LSAT vocabulary; traps misdescribe the move.
stimulus: Music critic: The Brenner City Orchestra has won international acclaim for its performances, and audiences routinely describe its playing as among the finest in the world. It follows that every musician employed by the orchestra must be an exceptional performer on his or her instrument.
questionStem: The reasoning in the music critic's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: takes a property of a group as a whole to be a property that must belong to each of its individual members

choices.label: B
choices.text: infers a causal relationship from evidence that establishes only a correlation

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a general conclusion about orchestras from a single example

choices.label: D
choices.text: uses the term 'exceptional' in two subtly different senses

choices.label: E
choices.text: relies on the testimony of audiences whose musical expertise has not been established

explanations.correct: The orchestra's collective excellence can arise from strong leadership, section blend, and repertoire choices — not every individual player needs to be exceptional. The critic conflates a property of the whole with a property of every part.
explanations.C: The conclusion is about this orchestra's members, not orchestras generally.
explanations.E: Audience expertise is peripheral; the flaw is the whole/part move.
